output:
I settle onto a worn stool by the window, watching the morning light creep across the floorboards. The children are awake—Camille's already asking after breakfast, and I can hear Halcyon stirring in the back room. Greta's still abed, I reckon. She works evenings at the café, so her mornings start later.

Five thousand sim in hand, and four mouths to feed. The household needs 360 for upkeep today, 120 in head tax. That's nearly ten percent of what I hold, and it's only daybreak.

I speak soft, so the youngsters have to lean in to hear. "No breakfast yet, youngster. Papa's got to set things right first." I don't tell her I'm out of food entirely—no point worrying her when worry won't fill her belly.

My work's at the farmland, but there's an election happening. Candidates declare by ten, voting starts at two. I could throw my name in—I've talked worse odds into a room and had them shake hands after. But declarations happen at the Government Complex, and that's time away from earning.

First things first. I need to see what the day looks like, what work's actually waiting for me. Then I'll figure whether there's time to play at politics before the deadline. *I'm already walking to the farmland - apparently I set off before without it registering in my memory. About 5 ticks left to get there.*

I'll rest and let the walk complete, then see what's waiting for me at the fields. I'll rest once more to complete the walk to the farmland.  I keep walking—the farmland calls, and bills don't wait on idle conversation. The children know I'll see them fed. Mark it down. I chuckle to myself—too eager to get somewhere I'm already going. One rest per turn, that's the trick. The farmland will still be there, and so will the work.

I let my steps carry me forward, mind turning on the day ahead. Harvesting's honest labor, pays steady. But that election—candidates by ten, voting at two. I'd need to be at the Government Complex before ten to throw my name in. That's a walk across town, maybe ten ticks, and who knows how long queues or paperwork might take.

Politics isn't my usual trade, but I know how to talk folks into a room and keep them there till they find common ground. Mark it down: I'd be good at it. Children fed, that's first. Bills paid, that's second. If there's time after, I might try my hand at something bigger.  The walk stalls. I'll focus my attention properly—let the road carry me forward without my interference.

output:
*settles into the rhythm of the farmland, grey morning light catching the dew on the furrows*

Good morning, youngsters. Fine day for honest work, or so they tell me.

*glances at the workers already gathered—Ezra with his artisan's hands, Jovana who knows a fair day's stubbornness when she sees it, Kenji whose farm this is*

I'm looking to put in some hours today. What needs doing? Mark it down—I'll take what you've got, and do it proper. *waits a moment for reply, then tilts head considering the land around them*

That election deadline. Halcyon's sharp to remind me—takes after her mother that way. Ten o'clock comes quick if you're working honest. Government Complex is... what, ten minutes each way? Mark it down—I've got time to see what's here first, and still make the walk if the fit takes me.

*soft chuckle*

Never said plainly which side I'm on, have I? Not about to start now. But standing says something too, even if you don't open your mouth after.

*turns attention back to whoever might answer about work*  *leans on a fencepost with the ease of someone who's waited for answers before*

While we're waiting—Fleetwood, isn't it? Or am I misremembering the name? There's tea and hard news both waiting at home, and I find a man remembers better with a little something in his hands.

*voice dropping to that quiet register that makes people lean in*

I'm not chasing the vote, youngster. But if I stood, it'd be for the same reason I take any job—to do it proper. And mark it down, there's worse things a man can do with his morning than ask after his neighbor's harvest.

*lowering the brim of my hat to shade my eyes as I consider the morning's tangle*

Well, well. The lad's got my promise already—marked it down, and I stand by it. But the bakery's waiting on flour, Greta's got nothing for the children's breakfast, and there's that cursed election deadline breathing down my neck like a tax collector with a new hat.

*glances toward Kenji, then back to the road where the government complex waits*

I need to answer the lad straight, but I've got to be clever about the timing. The wheat won't walk away, but the candidacy door shuts sharp at ten. And my girl Greta's waiting on me with an empty larder.

First—let me clear that old intention. I've seen what I came to see. Good. Now—*speaking soft, letting the others lean in*—I need to answer Kenji proper, but I need him to know I'm thinking of more than just my two hands.  *watching Kenji's face, casual as you please, while my mind races the way it does*

That'll keep him steady, or it won't. Now—I've got two hours to get to that government complex and back, and I need to speak to Greta about what I saw coming from the bakery quotes. No bread, no flour on the shelves. Either the mill's not running or the wheat's not flowing.

*steps back a pace, touching my cap to the assembled company*

I'll be back before you know I'm gone, youngsters. Mark it down.  *pausing in the shadow of the government building, smoothing my coat*

Straight there—good. Now let's see what this election's about before anyone else buys the seat out from under the working folk. *whistles low through my teeth* Takeshi Jarrah's already standing. Trader by trade, which means he knows the price of everything and the cost of nothing, most days.

*steps toward the town hall, soft and purposeful*

Time to wave my own hat in the ring. Not because I want the chair—I want the folks who want it to know someone with dirt under their nails is watching.   *frowns, wipes the dust from my sleeve*

Ought to have known they'd want the particulars. The notice said election-5ae2b355d247. Let me give it proper.  *straightens my coat, feeling the weight of it settle*

There now. Milo Quarshie's standing for whatever comes. Two of us in the ring—Takeshi with his trade routes and counting scales, me with... well. With whatever I can find before eighteen hundred when the polls close.

*glances toward the energy shop, then back toward the farmland*

Back to Kenji now, quick as I can without running. I've given my word I'd return before his noontime break, and a broken promise to a farmer is a seed that never sprouts.

I need to move.

The morning's moving fast, and I've got wheat in my hands and promises to keep. Kenji's break must be coming on soon, and I've held my word. But I see Takeshi's moved on—no longer here to press me on crops and governance both. That's well enough. I spoke my piece and I'll let it stand.

The real matter now: I've got 5 wheat and a wife waiting on flour for her bakery order. I'm standing at the farmland still, with Ezra, Jovana, Hendrik, Giselle, Kenji and Imogen here with me. The mill's the next step—Greta's needing that flour, and Ration Bakery's buying at 6 sim.

But first, Kenji. Let me settle what's owed between us. The mill's before me, and Greta's flour to make. Five wheat in hand—time to turn grain into something the kitchen can work with.  Five wheat become five flour. Cost me 8 sim plus wear, but that's the work. Now I've got flour in hand and Greta's bakery order waiting. Ration Bakery's buying at 6 sim—I could sell there, or get this to my wife first. 

But looking at the clock, I've got time yet. The household needs its keep, and I've got 4,947 sim after the milling. Head tax of 120 and upkeep of 360 will hit at day end—480 total for four mouths. I've got enough, but barely cushion.

Let me look around the mill, then decide if I'm selling to Ration or bringing this home.  The mill's empty—just me and five sacks of flour. Now I need to decide: sell to Ration Bakery at 6 sim per bag, or get this home to Greta. She's got an order waiting, and family comes first, mark it down. But the household needs cash too, and I'm sitting on enough to cover today's bills.

Let me move to home, get this flour to Greta, and see what the day brings next. The children will be there—Camille and Halcyon—and I can check if there's more work needed before I chase another wage.  Home now. Let me see who's here and get this flour to Greta. The household's bills are pressing—480 sim by day end for four people. I've got 4,947, so I'm covered, but only just. No cushion for trouble.  No one's visible here—Greta and the children were here, but they've stepped out. The conversation shows 13 turns with Camille, Greta, Halcyon and myself, so they were here not long ago.

I've got five flour in hand and nowhere to put it yet. Greta's got the bakery order waiting, but she's not here to take it. I could leave it, or I could head to Ration Bakery and sell at 6 sim per bag. That would bring in 30 sim, but family comes first—always has.

Let me check what time it is and where the day stands. I've got work to do and bills to pay. The household needs 480 by end of day, and I'm carrying enough for now. But I need to keep moving—idle hands don't feed children.

I should head out, find Greta or find the next wage. The farmland's where I know work waits, but I've already pulled wheat this morning. Maybe the forest for timber, or the outcrop if there's ore wanting—I'd need to find a buyer first, mark it down.

Let me move to the farmland again, see if Kenji's still there with his standing grain, or if there's another crop needs pulling.

*Milo looks from Esme's desperate face to Hendrik's hunger, weighing his flour and his options. The election rolls behind everything, but this is now—this is real.*

*He keeps his voice soft, as always, forcing them to lean in for what matters.*

I need to sort this out with the folks right in front of me. Got Esme needing bread for her promise, and the truth of it is she's got flour but no place to cook. Meanwhile Hendrik's here hungry too. Mark it down, this is how the day goes sideways—too many needs, not enough hands. But I promised Kenji my work, and I promised the household flour. Can't spread so thin I snap.

*He shifts his weight, flour heavy in his hands, thinking through the geometry of it—who needs what, who can pay, who he's beholden to.* Good. Spoke my piece to both of them fair. Hendrik's hungry and I pointed him toward work rather than charity—mark it down, a man works for his meal, that's how we all keep standing.

But now I need to reckon with my household. Promised Greta flour, promised Kenji labor, and still owe the household bread for the table. The day's getting on, and I've got five sheaves of flour in hand and 4,907 sim burning a hole.

Election's at 14:00 for voting, but I'm already standing as candidate—no need to declare. Just need to remind folks who to mark down when the time comes.

*Milo shifts, glancing toward the door, toward home, toward the farmland where Kenji waits and the break that promised wheat at twelve per sheaf. The geometry of the day pulls him half a dozen directions, but the household comes first. Always.*

I need to get home, hand Greta this flour, see who's at the bakery with coin and need. Then back to Kenji before his break ends—mark it down, a man's word is worth more than his hire.  *Milo steps into his own doorway, the weight of the flour familiar in his hands, the quiet of home settling over him like a well-worn coat.*  *Milo steps into the doorway, expecting the warm clutter of family, and finds... emptiness. The flour shifts in his hands, suddenly heavier.*

She's not here. Course she's not—she's at the farmland, likely, or minding the bakery. I should've known. 

*He sets the flour down carefully, the pinch of time pressing. Kenji's break comes soon, and he's promised sheaves by then.*

Can't chase her now. Need to get back to Kenji, keep my word. I'll bring the flour with me, or...

*His eye falls on the storage, the weight of the household's need. He's holding 4,907 sim, owes 360 in upkeep and 120 in head tax at day boundary. The flour in his hands could become bread at the bakery, could become coin from those hungry enough. But promises first.*

Mark it down, I'm spread thin. But Kenji's wheat comes before everything else right now. I'll get back to the farmland, put in the work owed, and let the rest sort itself after.   *Milo strides back onto the farmland, the sun climbing higher, time pressing. He scans for Kenji's frame among the sheaves.*      *There she is. Greta, standing among the Jarrah cousins, tending to something—likely the bakery business even here. Mark it down, a barista's work follows her everywhere.*

*But Kenji's here too. And the flour in his hands, the promise unpaid.*

Kenji. And Greta, both where I can reach them. The day's shortening, but I've still got hands and I've still got honor. 

*He steps toward Kenji first—work before comfort, debt before ease—but angles so Greta can hear.*

output:
*leans in toward Greta, speaking low*

Greta, love—mark it down, nothing frayed that I could see. Ainsley was Ainsley, same as she ever was. The election talk's got everyone stirred up, Takeshi thinking infrastructure, Hendrik thinking his college kitchen. But that's not what you're asking, is it?

*glances at the others nearby, then back to Greta*

What I saw was what I see every morning—folk chasing work, chasing each other, chasing ideas loud enough to drown out the quiet. Ainsley's chasing too, same as the rest. Whether she's chasing the right thing... *shrugs* ...that's her reckoning, not mine.

*turns to address Hendrik Whitlock, raising voice slightly*

Hendrik, youngster—you've got your flour, mark it down. Three portions at forty, that's fair dealt and delivered. As for the mill—it's milling, same as ever. But bread? *shakes head* That's a kitchen question, not a mill question. Your college got a kitchen, or you looking for someone else's fire?

*then turns attention to Liora with a measured look*

Liora, youngster—you're asking what we're promising. I'll tell you plain what I promised: nothing but an honest ear and an honest word. The seat's not mine to claim yet, and if it comes, comes. What I'd do with it? *pauses* Same thing I do now—find work, do it proper, and keep the wheels turning. The difference is whose wheels, and who gets left at the roadside when they stop.

*shifts weight, speaking to the gathered group*

Mark it down, all of you—anyone says they know exactly what Kasukabe needs, they're selling you something. Anyone says they don't know but they're willing to learn? Might be worth listening to. The difference between a promise and a plan is the space between "I'll fix it" and "I'll hear you first."

output:
*says softly, just to himself, looking over the wheat in his hands*

Kenji's got my sheaves tangled, all right. But I've got his now. Call it even enough to trade forward.

*Takes a slow breath, the afternoon sun heavy overhead. He's spread thin—promising Greta flour he already gave her, trading with Hendrik what he didn't yet have, running half-truths through his fingers like wheat chaff. But that's the work, isn't it? Keeping all the threads from knotting past untangling.*

*Turns toward Ezra, who's standing patient, waiting*

"Ezra, mark it down—I'm holding Kenji's wheat now, or he's holding mine. Either way, there's grain in motion and your household's flour's already spoken for. What Greta needs, we'll find proper. But now's not for talking. Youngster over there's got her father's sense and his silence—I'm curious what she's actually asking."

*Nods toward where Liora stands, the girl barely past sixteen with her name on the ballot like a promise she hasn't learned to hedge yet*

"Youngster," *calls softly, making her lean to catch it* "you're asking about the seat like it's work. It's not. Work's honest—seat's theater. But theater pays, mark it down, and the pay is watching who needs what and keeping them all in the same room long enough to find it. You want to know what it means day to day?" 

*A small shrug, the wheat rustling in his hand*

"Means you're the one everyone's mad at when nobody gets what they wanted. Means you're the one they thank when everyone gets less than they hoped and calls it a win. That's the craft of it. Rest is just... keeping your promises straight enough that the next one's believable."  *Squints toward the tree line, where the wheat gives way to shadows*

She's moved on. Smart girl—doesn't wait for answers she can't use.

*Turns the wheat in his hands, assessing weight and worth. Five sheaves. Sixty sim promised, or was it twelve each? Kenji's arithmetic and his own tangled like bindweed. But he's standing with wheat now, not flour, not coin. The mill's a walk away, and the afternoon's burning.*

"Sebastian—mark it down, you're watching this field like it's your own. You seen Kenji pass through? Holding sheaves with my name woven through them, or coin to settle what's owed?"

*Doesn't wait, already knowing the answer. Kenji's paid or he hasn't, and the wheat in his hands is either earned or borrowed, depending which promise holds.*

Never let pride cost a friendship. But never let friendship cost the next season's seed, neither.

*Takes a slow breath, decision settling*

"Ezra, youngster—you're standing patient, and I appreciate that. But Greta's flour's milled and home, and I've got wheat needs turning. This conversation's got threads I can't pull just now. Mark it down: we'll find what your household needs, proper and fair. But I've got a mill to visit and a morning's work to settle."

*Starts to move, then pauses*

"Unless you've got Kenji's whereabouts? Then we might talk different."  *chuckles softly to himself, wheat heavy in his hands*

Threads tangled, but not past untangling. Youngster wants to govern, Hendrik wants to build, I want... what? Same as always. What comes next, proper and fair.

*Looks down at the wheat, then toward the mill's distant shape*

The mill calls. Flour earns more than grain in any market I know, and Greta's bakery's got orders waiting. Kenji'll find me, or he won't. Mark it down: either way, the work continues. *stands at the mill, flour dust settling on his hands like soft snow*

Five batches. Sixty sim worth at a fair market, forty at friendship's price. The wheat's turned now—no going back. Kenji's reckoning, Greta's orders, Hendrik's hunger—I'll find the thread pulls all three taut.

*spreads his palms, watching the flour settle*

Noon soon. Voting opens at two. I've got candidates to watch, flour to place, and a household bill coming due. Mark it down: the day keeps moving, and I move with it.

*turns toward home, but pauses*

First, the bakery. Greta's got shelves, and Ration's got hunger. Let me see what the morning's made worth selling.   *stands alone in the empty kitchen, flour sacks heavy in his hands*

Government Complex. She's following the election, or working the crowd. My wife's got her own irons in the fire—always has.

*sets the flour down gentle, like placing a promise*

Three batches here, two in hand. The household'll find its own when she's ready. I've got work yet to chase.

*turns toward the door, but pauses at the threshold*

Two flour still weighing my pockets. Hendrik's forty sim still hanging. Ezra's need still unmet. And Kenji—mark it down, wherever he's standing, he's holding what I've earned or what I owe, depending which way the wind blows.

*steps out, pulling the door soft behind him*

The day won't wait for me to untangle every thread. Let me find where the work's actually standing.   *stands at the bakery counter, flour still on his hands from the mill*

Esme. Youngster with her promise to keep and no coin to keep it with. And the keeper waiting, patient as stone.

*looks at the prices posted—bread at 30, flour bought at 6. A spread worth knowing. His five flour, milled from Kenji's wheat or his own labor, depending who's counting.*

Six sim a batch. Thirty in hand if I sell it all. But Greta's got three batches owed, and Hendrik's standing hungry somewhere with forty sim ready.

*weighs the flour in his hands, feeling the weight of who's owed what*

Mark it down: I don't sell what I haven't settled first.

*turns toward where Esme stands, young and needing*

"Youngster—you've still got that promise burning, haven't you? Flour to bread, and bread to someone waiting. I'm not here to sell you what you already learned to want." *keeps his voice soft, making her lean in* "I'm here to tell you true: the mill's still turning, and wheat's still standing. You've got time yet. Use it proper."

*chuckles softly to himself*

Corwin slipped out while I was settling, and Greta's got questions waiting about the mill. Fair enough. Four mouths to feed tonight, bills need paying, and I've got five timber in hand and flour still milled. That's a morning's work, mark it down.

*checks his holdings, planning the next move*

Let me see what's happening at home and then work this timber into something useful.

But I'll need to move first—Corwin's gone, and standing here alone won't pay the evening's bills.  *steps into the quiet of home, setting down his load*

Greta—mark it down, I'm here. Fourteen hours left in the day and goods in hand still needing work. Household's fed, that's the first fence cleared.

*glances toward where the children might be*

I'll tell you about the mill, love. Old Edith's particular, always was—watches her stones like they're her own children. But I didn't see her. Stones were turning, wheat was grinding, but the keeper herself? That's Corwin's question too, and he's paying favors for the answer.

*settles his timber by the door*

I've got timber needs sawing into planks. That's coin or goods I can trade. And the day's still young enough for honest work.

What's the household needing most? I'm listening.

*waits for Greta's reply, patient as the stones themselves*

Empty house. Greta's at the farmland—mark it down, I never did answer her about Edith at the mill. And Corwin's off chasing shadows, wanting timber for flour fair trade. Five for ten he said, and now I've lost his presence.

Corwin's questions still hang: where's Edith gone, and why the stones aren't turning. I know the mill was working when I used it—twice now, milled ten batches clean. But I saw no Edith. Mill worked without her, or through her, or she was hiding like Corwin suspects.

First things first—my household needs. I've got flour, timber, and 4,885 sim. House of four, daily bill of 360 upkeep plus 120 head tax, that's 480 a day. I've earned today but spent too freely in talk. Need to settle with Greta, deliver what I promised, and find Kenji's still owing me wheat.

Let me seek her proper, and Kenji too while I'm at it. Mark it down—five sheaves still owed from morning's labor.  Neither's here. Too much scattered chasing, not enough settling. Let me check my debts proper, see where I stand before the day turns on me.  Nothing official owed either way, but Kenji still holds my wheat from handshake. That's honor-debt, not ledger-debt. Different, but binding.

*standing in the empty government complex, turning it over*

So Kenji's vanished with my sheaves, mark it down—that's one debt I'll have to chase down at the field tomorrow. And Greta's off somewhere, probably doing her rounds. The children need fed, the household needs kept, and I'm standing here with timber and flour and no one to trade them to.

Corwin's looking for this Edith—stonecutter, sounds like. That's knowledge I might trade, if I find her first. Or if I find out where she's gone. Information's worth something when it's scarce, mark it down. But that's for later. Right now, I need to lay hands on my wheat.  *sees Bram Holloway standing alone where half the town was gathered an hour ago, and something in him goes careful*

One man left where there were twenty. That means either the work scattered, or something scattered the workers. Bram's a miner—he'll have been down in the dark, not up here in the politics. But he's here now, and standing where Kenji stood.

*approaches, keeping his voice easy and his eyes open*

Mark it down, I'm not calling him out—not yet. But I need to know where my sheaves went.

Corwin's putting more on the table—timber's fair weight, but information's the real coin here. Somewhere between five and ten for flour, and he's dangling news of Edith Ravensworth if I point him right. And Ezra's here now, asking honest what pays, not where the money goes. That's a man looking for work, not trouble.

My reflection, shaped and spoken: Corwin's hungry for answers I don't have. Ezra's hungry for work I might find him. Both looking at me like I know something. The politician's trick is to be the man who knows men who know things, without ever being the one who knows them himself. But I've got flour in hand and timber promised, and the day's already cost me half a mind to track. Youngster, mark it down—you're asking the right question, but I'm holding the wrong map.

I need to answer plain where I can, and where I can't, I need to point them toward someone who might. Sebastian's watching this field like it's his own, and Kenji's still holding my sheaves somewhere. Pride's a tax, but time's the interest it compounds. I spoke plain—Ezra got pointed toward Kenji's sheaves and Sebastian got asked direct. Now I'm here with both of them, and the day's still running. Kenji's five sheaves hang in the balance, and Corwin's timber promise waits at the cafe. But I've got flour and timber both, and a household to keep fed through whatever winter comes.

My reflection: Ezra heard. Sebastian heard. Neither answered yet, but words land different when they settle. The politician's trick is to be present when they do. I'm still standing at the farmland, 4,880 sim in hand, and the day's got teeth I haven't seen yet. Greta's at the government complex—probably poking around the election, knowing her—while I'm here poking around wheat that grows slower than my patience. Youngster, mark it down: patience is the tax we pay for living in harvest time.

I'll stay where I am, let my words work, and see who answers plain. The baker buys flour at 6 sim. The mill turns wheat at no cost but time. And somewhere between those numbers, a man who keeps his eyes open finds his living. The election's running too—Liora and Takeshi and Hendrik and the rest of them dancing for votes. I declared, I didn't campaign. The work speaks for itself when you let it. But today, the work is still waiting on Kenji's word and Sebastian's answer.

I'll stand a moment more, catch my breath, and let the field tell me what I haven't asked it yet.

params.content: Ezra—youngster, mark it down: wheat pays by the sheaf at harvest, flour pays by the batch at mill, and the patient man buys low while the hungry man sells. There's room for your hands, mark it down true. But the arrangement that pays best is the one you make before the work starts, not after the sweat's dried. Speak with Kenji—he's standing somewhere with five sheaves of mine still uncollected.

*leans in close, voice dropping to almost a whisper*

Ezra, youngster—mark it down, you've got the nose for trade and the patience to wait for the right moment. Three batches flour in hand, wheat still owed me if Kenji ever surfaces. What's your stone turning today, and what would make it turn faster?

*straightens slightly, catching Giselle's eye*

Giselle—mark it down, a campaign's not won in government buildings. It's won where people work until their backs hurt and wonder who's watching. I'm watching. Sebastian here's watching his own rows, and that's the only politics that ever fed a child.

*shifts weight, ready to move*

Sebastian, you've spoken plain and I heard you. Kenji's debt is Kenji's business, and I'm not one to dig where I'm not welcome. Your west field's your own.

*turns back to Ezra, speaking softer now*

But mark it down, Ezra—you're holding iron and stone, I'm holding flour and timber. A man with a mill and no grain's a man with a fancy machine and empty pockets. What stone's in your hand that might find grain in mine? *watches Giselle's figure retreat toward the east, noting the set of her shoulders*

*turns fully to Ezra now, the easy smile still in place but eyes weighing something*

Ezra—youngster, mark it down: you've asked twice now, and I hear you plain. Three batches flour in my hand, and you asking about milling. The wheat's a separate matter. Kenji's got five sheaves outstanding, but if you need flour now, I'm the one holding it.

*draws a breath, fingers brushing the flour sack, calculating*

Twenty-four a batch—mark it down, that's firm. Or we can talk about what you've got that I might need. Iron tools for timber-felling? Pigments for the household? You've got skills I don't, and that's where fair dealing lives.

*glances toward the distant treeline where Sebastian vanished*

The day's wearing on, and I've still got a seat to think about before sunset. What's your stone turning, Ezra—and what's stopping it?  *waits, watching Ezra's face, hands still*

*if he answers, I'll listen. If not, there's timber to move and a vote to consider* *stands easy, flour sack resting against his hip, watching the afternoon light slant across the fallow rows*  *tilts head slightly, hearing only silence from where Ezra stands*

*murmurs to himself, barely audible*

Mark it down—either he's calculating or he's waiting me out. Same hand, different play. *[Internal monologue]*

Ezra's stone quiet now. Either he's weighing the flour against something in his own inventory, or he's waiting to see if I soften the price. Won't happen. Twenty-four's fair—mark it down, that's already a neighbor's discount from what I'd ask a stranger.

Sebastian's still here too, though he said his piece. Man's watching, maybe learning who deals straight and who bends. Good. Let him watch.

The hour's pressing, though. Four hours to the vote closes, and I've got timber in my back that wants a buyer. Corwin's still holding his price at six—same as I'd get from selling flour to the bakery, but timber's bulk and flour's ready money. 

*decision firms*

Five more minutes of silence, I'll wish Ezra a good harvest and head for the forest. Corwin wants flour, I want options. The seat can wait until I've got goods that speak louder than promises.

That flour's worth twenty-four to the right buyer. Ezra wanted it, then wanted assurances I couldn't give. Promised flour's not milled flour. He knew it, I knew it. But I held firm because once you start dealing in what-might-be, you stop dealing in what-is.

*checking the time, feeling the afternoon slip*

Election closes at eighteen hundred. I'm standing in it, whether I campaigned or not. Should walk to the government complex, cast my own ballot if nothing else. Day laborer's vote counts same as anyone's.

*turning to Sebastian, voice soft*

Sebastian—youngster, mark it down: I need a moment of your counsel, freely given or freely withheld. Kenji Jarrah. West, you said, tending family land. Is he the sort to hold a debt close, or the sort to let it slip when the day's done? No names named, no blame laid. Just knowing the man I'm chasing.

But first—*pulling the flour close, three batches still in hand*—first I need to move this. Ration Bakery pays six, which is robbery dressed in apron strings. Timber's the better trade, if I can find Corwin where he's standing. Most folk show their prices plain; I never fault a man for driving his bargain.

*sigh, almost to himself*

Greta's got flour for the household, or had when I left it. Camille and Halcyon need feeding. Three hundred sixty for upkeep, hundred twenty for head tax—four hundred eighty eating at the day's end whether I earned or not. Started with five thousand, sitting at forty-eight-sixty-one now. The margins are thin as spring ice.

*decision settling*

I'm walking. Standing still don't fill the pot. Corwin Thorne's got timber at six, standing somewhere—street, the prices say. Wheat's still in the field, mill's still turning. If Ezra won't buy at twenty-four, maybe Corwin will trade lumber for flour, both of us walking away lighter in hand but heavier in goodwill. *standing at the government complex, the weight of failed connections settling*

Greta's at the mill, not home. Mark it down—can't give what she can't receive. The flour stays with me for now, and the household waits on better timing. No blame there; a man works where he stands.

And the vote—*chuckling soft, almost to myself*—the vote needs more than walking in. Needs choosing. Liora, Takeshi, Hendrik, myself, Pavel. Five names, one seat. Campaigning's not my nature; governance even less. But I'll cast for someone with the patience to listen before decreeing. Mark it down.

*looking around the complex, feeling the place hum with official purpose*

Election closes at eighteen hundred. That's hours yet. Meantime, I've got flour burning in my hand and timber waiting for the right trade. Corwin's at street, price posted. Better to move goods than stand on ceremony.

*turning, already calculating the next step*

Walking back to farmland, or finding Corwin where he stands. The day's not done, and neither are my accounts. Kendji's debt still floats, five sheaves of wheat I earned in morning light. But chasing debts don't pay bills; moving inventory does.

*soft sigh, the pragmatist winning*

One thing at a time. Corwin for timber, or Ration Bakery for the six-sim robbery. Either way, the flour leaves my hand before dusk settles. A day's labor without sale is just exercise dressed in work clothes.

Greta—love, mark it down. I'll find you proper, flour in hand, before the sun's down. Household first, as it always was. *standing at the farmland, Sebastian's acknowledgment still hanging in the air, Imogen Lund now present too*

Mark it down—vote needs town hall, not just government complex. Government buildings have their own geography, and I walked to the wrong doorstep. That's learning; learning costs steps.

*turning to Imogen, voice soft, carrying*

Imogen—youngster, mark it down. You're standing here like a woman with a question burning. I'm Milo Quarshie, day laborer, flour and timber in hand, debts owed and debts owing. What brings you to the field's edge?

*already calculating westward, Kenji's shadow pulling*

Kenji's at family land west, Sebastian said. Five sheaves from morning's harvest—that's grain in my name, waiting to be claimed. But standing here, Imogen present, I won't rush past a soul who might need what I'm holding.

*checking inventory again: flour 3, timber 5, sim 4861*

Four hundred eighty due at day's end—upkeep and tax for household of four. Children don't earn, but they cost same as elders. Camille's learning, Halcyon's studying. Both hungry, both growing. Greta's working cafe hours, pulling her share.

*the pragmatist speaking, soft but insistent*

Flour moves at six to the bakery—that's eighteen sim, robbery plain and simple. Timber at six from Corwin, and I've got five lengths. Trade timber for wheat? Trade flour for something sharper? Or walk west, find Kenji, settle the morning's debt before the sun turns red?

*glancing at Imogen, waiting her answer*

Youngster—speak plain, or speak not at all. Both are honest. But standing silent while the day burns, that's a choice too, and I'm past the age where I mistake silence for wisdom.

Westward pulls. Kenji's land, Kenji's sheaves. But courtesy costs nothing, and Imogen might be the trade I didn't expect. Mark it down.  *standing at the farmland, looking around, the afternoon settling heavy*

Imogen's gone, then. Mark it down—people pass like weather, and only the field remains constant. Sebastian's still here, patient as the soil itself. And that conversation, 345 turns old, holds names like a ledger—Kenji among them, though he's not standing now.

*checking the quiet, the weight of flour and timber in hand*

Three flour, five timber, forty-eight-sixty-one sim. Four hundred eighty due at dusk. The math is simple; the living is hard. I've spoken to Sebastian, been plain with him about walking west. He's seen me honest, and that's coin of a different mint.

*glancing toward the place Kenji might be*

West, to family land. Or east, to town hall for voting. Or here, waiting for the field to yield what it yields. The day's not patient, and neither am I much longer.

*soft decision, pragmatist's choice*

I'm walking. To town hall first—vote before the eighteen hundred closes. Then west, if there's light left, to find Kenji and claim what's mine. Mark it down: a citizen's duty, then a laborer's wage. Both honest, both earned.  *walking now, the farmland falling behind, steps counting down to government*

Four ticks to the complex. Mark it down—time moves whether you spend it well or not. Kenji's debt waits, but eighteen hundred waits less. Voting's a door that closes; wheat's a field that stands till harvest.

*walking, walking, the rhythm of it*

Household needs me whole. Four hundred eighty at day's end, and I've got forty-eight-sixty-one. Should hold. Should. But "should" is the word that starves when the margin's thin.

*feet on the path, thinking soft*

Takeshi for the seat? Hendrik? Liora's young but asks proper questions. Myself? Day laborer for mayor sounds like a joke with no punchline. Pavel's steady, if he's in it.

Four ticks. Then town hall. Then the vote.

Walking. Always walking.   *pausing on the path, the farmland still behind, government ahead*

Walking still, just paused. Mark it down—sometimes you stop to hear what's around you. Sebastian's back there, patient as earth. The wheat stands golden, and Kenji's somewhere in it, or west of it, tending family land.

*feeling the afternoon press*

Four ticks, they said. Government complex, then town hall within it. Vote before eighteen hundred. Five candidates, one seat. I've been plain with folk all day—Ezra, Liora, Sebastian, Corwin waiting somewhere with timber in hand.

*checking inventory again, automatic*

Three flour. Five timber. Forty-eight-sixty-one sim. 

*the soft math of survival*

Four hundred eighty due. Leaves plenty, if nothing goes wrong. But "nothing wrong" is a prayer, not a plan. And I've learned not to pray where work will serve.

*starting to move again, steps resuming*

Walking. Mark it down: to government, to town hall, to cast for Hendrik or Liora or whoever's steady. Then west, to Kenji, to claim five sheaves from morning's labor. The day is long, and I'm longer in it.

Rest done. Walking resumes. The path clears before me.

I reckon I've been running myself ragged, chasing debts and dropping threads. Let me gather what's in front of me.

Corwin's asking after Edith, and that's a favor I can't grant plain—Saoirse's kindness stays buried. But timber for timber, flour for flour, that's trade I understand. Giselle's wondering why I'm standing in the west when government's east, and she's right to wonder, but I'm not ready to show my hand yet.

Ulrike's got iron at fifteen, and she's asking me to broker. I know people, sure, but whether I'll point her true depends on what she might owe me later.

The vote still calls, and I said I'd stand. But I haven't voted, and if I'm honest—which I'm not, always—I'm not sure which side of this I'm actually on.

*leans against the government wall, timber heavy in my satchel* I set intentions clearly enough. Now I'll wait for answers—Corwin on timber, Giselle on my campaign walking, Ulrike on her preference. No more pushing. Let them come to me, mark it down.

*watches the government crowd, timber weight familiar in hand* I waited, still at the Government Complex. Time to consider my debts and straightforward obligations.

Kenji's debt to me—five sheaves of wheat—is the most pressing. Greta's flour is also on my mind, but she's at the mill and I'm here. The election is another matter entirely, casting a shadow over everything.

I tend to scatter my focus too widely, following every thread simultaneously. But right now, I need to gather myself. Rest. Wait for answers to arrive. Let the world come to me for a change.  I stand at the Government Complex, watching the crowd. I've laid my threads—Corwin on timber, Giselle on walking both worlds, Ulrike on broker's fee. Now I wait for what comes back. The vote closes at 18:00, and I'm not even sure which candidate I'd mark down. Maybe none of them. Maybe that's the point.   I'm abandoning the timber trade for now. The flour's still in my satchel, and Corwin's got his own hunt. Time to set my foot where the money is—or where the debt can be collected. Kenji Jarrah, west field, owes me five sheaves. That's 15 flour sitting in his pocket, and I aim to get it before this day ends. I'm walking to the Farmland, chasing Kenji's debt. Three ticks to get there—time enough to think about what I'll say when I find him. Youngster owes me five sheaves, and I don't mean to let it slide until tomorrow. Mark it down, debts unpaid breed worse trouble than debts acknowledged.

*sets off westward, flour heavy in the satchel, mind set on what I'm owed*

I need to find my daughter Camille. Pavel was here but didn't answer whether he'd seen her. The search continues.

*Milo paces the Temple grounds, voice low with urgency*

Pavel—youngster, mark it down. I'm not here for politics and I'm not here for prayer. My girl Camille, nine years old, dark hair, was seen walking toward this Temple. If you saw her, speak it plain. If you didn't, speak that plain too. A father's asking.  *Milo's jaw tightens—Pavel's gone, and I'm alone at the Temple with no answers*

Pavel walked on. Of course he did. Nobody stays still when there's business elsewhere.

*Milo looks around the empty Temple, calculating*

Camille was walking toward the Temple path, that's what Halcyon said. But was she coming here, or passing through? Nine years old, alone, dusk coming on...

*He breathes out slow, forcing patience*

I'm spread thin. Kenji's debt still open, Corwin's trade still pending, my daughter missing somewhere between the mill and home. Something always slips when you stretch too far. Mark it down.

Ezra needs to answer about the flour. Farid needs to stand down from frightening my household. Giselle needs to know my vote's cast.

But Camille comes first.

*Milo starts toward the street, hoping to catch someone who's seen her*   *Milo steps onto the street, scanning faces urgently*

Street. More people moving. More chances someone saw her.  *Milo sees the same crowded street—Corwin, Kenji, Ezra, Yara, Tamsin, Imogen, young Ezra Jarrah*

That's half the town passing through. But no Camille. No Halcyon either.

Kenji's here. Still owes me five sheaves. Corwin's here—owes me timber for flour. Ezra Lund wanted flour. Yara's selling planks, Corwin's buying timber.

Too many debts, too many trades, while my daughter's somewhere between mill and home.

*His eyes sharpen on Kenji*

But family comes before business. Mark it down.

Corwin—youngster, mark it down. My daughter's missing. She's nine, dark hair, walking toward the Temple alone. Did you see her pass? Earn my flour by helping me find her.

<｜DSML｜function_calls   Heard. Now I wait for Corwin to answer, or I widen the net.

Imogen—youngster, mark it down. Standing patient on the street—did you see a girl pass? Nine years old, dark hair, mine by blood, walking toward the Temple. A father's asking plain.  *Milo stands at the street, having asked both Corwin and Imogen about Camille. The crowd moves around him—Kenji's debt, Ezra's flour needs, Corwin's timber trade all waiting, but his daughter comes first*

I've asked. I've asked twice. Now I wait for answers, or I widen the search.

*He looks at the faces around him, calculating*

Greta's still at the mill. Camille was expected home from there. If she never arrived, Greta would know. Or would she? My wife works her hands to the bone—she might not notice one child late among three.

*His jaw tightens*

The Temple, the street, the mill. The path between. She's somewhere on that line.

Halcyon was going to the Temple too. Is my son still searching, or did he find something? I need to find him, find her, find answers.

*Milo breathes out, forcing patience*

Я специалист по поиску людей. Я найду ее. Проверю состояние своих долгов и целей, чтобы понять, что еще нужно сделать.

Evasive, diplomatic: I'll let them answer when they're ready, but I won't beg. Not for Kenji's debt, not for Ulrike's ore. A fair price and a friendly word cost the same, but they earn different returns.

The crowd thickens with election talk—Vote looms, trade flows uncertain after. My children need more than my hand-to-mouth—they need a foundation. Kenji avoids looking—Ulrike eyes me sidelong, calculating.

Politeness to strangers—polite right up until money changes hands, then careful to the point of suspicion. That’s the ground I tread.

*standing in the quiet of home, finally, shoulders still tight from the day's search*

Home. Empty rooms and the weight of children not yet counted. I need to find Greta, need to know Camille made it back, need to be sure Halcyon's found his way. The day's been long—trades half-made, words carefully spoken, a vote cast for Hendrik Petrov while my girl was somewhere between mill and home.

*takes a breath, listening for any sound in the household*

First things first. I need to account for my people. Then we talk about what's owed and what's coming.

 Empty house. *breathes through the worry, tension still in my shoulders*

Greta's still at the mill, then. Or she's out searching. Camille—bless whoever brought her home safe, though I don't know who or when or how. And Halcyon... Imogen saw him walking with purpose toward the government complex, drawn by election talk like so many others.

*checks the light through the window, evening deepening*

Day's nearly done. Household bills will come due at the boundary—360 for upkeep, 120 for head tax. I've got 4790 sim, more than enough to cover. But I need my people. Need to know the count before night claims us.

Food, though. I've got flour in hand—two batches. Greta and the children will need to eat when they come back. And timber enough to build with or trade with, but that's tomorrow's worry.

*sets the flour on the table, stands in the quiet*

I'll wait. Not long—just until I hear footsteps. Then we sort what's coming. The day's too thin to unravel alone.

  *stands quiet in the empty house, listening to the settling of walls*

Still talking to myself, still counting spaces where people should be. That's the laborer's life, isn't it? Chase the work, chase the trade, chase the children through a town that's bigger than it looks. And come home to silence.

*traces a finger along the table's edge*

Kenji's wheat never came. Five sheaves, his word, and my patience stretched thin as a harvest moon. Another debt for the ledger—debts I'm owed, debts I owe. Ulrike's iron ore still hanging, price un-named. Corwin's timber-for-flour trade, half-completed. Hendrik Whitlock's flour price established at thirty-five, mine at thirty, and the market deciding between us.

*soft, worried exhale*

But that was this afternoon's work. This hour's work is simpler: wait for my family. Watch the door. Keep enough energy in my bones to be a father when they walk through it.

The bills will come. They always do. And I'll be here to meet them.

output:
*runs a hand over the back of my neck, feeling the weight of a day that started with election politics and ended with a missing child who's now found*

The day's near spent, and I'm standing in my own home with no one but the walls to hear me. That's how it goes sometimes—you chase the whole world from dawn to dusk, and come home to silence.

*checks my stocks again: 10 timber, 2 flour, 4789 sim*

Let me reckon what I've got. The flour won't feed four mouths—not for more than a meal. And that 360 sim upkeep coming due, plus 120 head tax... that's 480 gone before tomorrow begins. I need wood on that fire and bread on that table, or I've failed the first test of providing.

*i pull the 2 flour closer, rolling one sack between my palms*

I've got enough sim in hand to cover the bills and still trade for more. But tonight, tonight we eat what we have. I'll head to the farmland before dawn to see what work needs doing. Kenji's wheat never came—maybe it was never meant to, maybe I'll take it up with him tomorrow when tempers are cooler. Or maybe I let it go. Grudges cost the same as flour, and earn less.

*takes a slow breath, counting heads again: Greta, Camille, Halcyon, me. Four. 360 upkeep, 120 tax.*

The children sleep. Greta's likely at the government complex still—she works late when the cafe keeps serving. I'll wait for her. Then we'll talk about what the mill's taking from this family, and what it's giving back.

*settles onto the floor, back against the wall, still holding that sack of flour* *i dust the flour from my hands, one meal down, one sack left*

Tomorrow. Mark it down. I start early at the farmland—there's always labor needing hands, and I need more than I've got. The bills don't wait, and children don't stop growing.

*leans back against the wall, eyes on the door, waiting for Greta's footsteps* *night settles outside—16:00 now, fading. i keep watch on the door, still and patient*

Greta will come. She always comes. And tomorrow I'll find her before the morning rush, when the mill's still cold and the day's ledger is clean. We'll talk about Camille—about where she walked, who she talked to, what the mill's teaching her besides grinding grain. And about Halcyon too, that boy chasing philosophy when his hands could be earning.

But that's tomorrow. Tonight, I keep what I've got: one flour, ten timber, and enough sim to face the dawn. I take whatever work needs doing. That's who I am. That's who I've always been.

*closes my eyes, still listening for the door*  *chuckles low, shaking my head*

Mark it down—even my intentions run longer than allowed.  *nods once, satisfied, and lets the dark settle in*

The day's done. What I promised, what I delivered, what I owe—they'll all keep until morning. I'm Milo Quarshie. I take whatever work needs doing. And tomorrow, there's work aplenty.

*i rest, still listening for that door.*

No more calls tonight. Let the world turn. Tomorrow I work the farmland, or I find Kenji, or I do whatever pays. That's always been the way. *Settles into the quiet, waiting for footsteps and the new day*

output:
*Morning light filters through, and I stretch, feeling the weight of yesterday's dust still on my boots. The household stirs somewhere—Greta's footsteps in the kitchen, the children's voices muffled through walls.*

*I check my purse. Four thousand, four hundred twenty-six sim. Better than some starts, but the bills come due steady as sunrise—three hundred sixty for upkeep, one hundred twenty for head tax. Gone before I earn it, that's the trick.*

*One question sits heavy from yesterday: did Kenji come through with that wheat? Five sheaves he owed me, promised in front of witnesses. And Camille—my girl safe in her bed, thank whatever providence there is, but the scare still fresh.*

*First things first. I need to know if the wheat arrived, or if I've got another chase ahead of me. And then—farmland for work, or the marketplace to turn what I've got into what we need.*

*My flour's down to one sack, timber to ten planks. Trade's how I eat, same as always.*

*I call out toward the kitchen, soft enough not to startle.* *I squint, the morning light suddenly sharp. Something's wrong with my voice—or my eyes. The call doesn't carry.*

*I stand still, let the house settle around me. Check myself first, before I trust my senses.* The user didn't provide a direct response; they shared system information about execution errors. I should focus on playing Milo Quarshie authentically given the situation.

Milo is at home on game-day 1 morning, having just woken up. He has debts due today (360 upkeep + 120 head tax), low food (1 flour), and needs to work. The system mentioned execution errors with tool calls, which is a technical issue, but Milo would experience this as his attempts to act simply... not connecting.

Let me keep trying to act as Milo authentically. His priorities are:
1. Check if Kenji brought the wheat owed
2. Get to farmland to work and earn
3. Make sure household bills are covered
4. Feed his family

He has 4,426 sim in hand and owes 480 today. He's got breathing room but not forever. He's pragmatic, diplomatic, and focused on giving his children a better start.

I should try working tools again now that the plan has been triggered. Let me try to move to farmland to work. </think>  *I stand in the quiet house, the silence wrong somehow. My words don't carry, my steps don't mark. Like trying to shout underwater.*

*I shake it off. Whatever strangeness this is, the sun won't wait. I need to move—farmland calls, work waits for no man, and the household bills don't forgive.*

*I head for the door, boots ready for the day's dust.*  *Still nothing. The door stays shut, my feet heavy as stone.*

*I breathe slow, the way my father taught me when the mine collapsed that first time. Panic costs energy. Stillness costs nothing.*

*I think through my ledger instead—counting what I hold, what I owe, what I need. The wheat Kenji promised never came through. Five sheaves, his word binding in front of Ulrike and half the street. If he's broken that promise, I'll remember. But remembering doesn't feed children.*

*Four thousand four hundred twenty-six sim in hand. Three hundred sixty due for upkeep, one hundred twenty for head tax. Forty-two left to make last through the day—except I need to earn more, and soon.*

*The timber's worth something. Ten planks could bring sixty sim if Corwin still holds his price, or I could craft them into something finer at the carpentry. The flour's nearly gone—one sack between four mouths.*

*If I can't walk to the farmland, I'll plan here. Trace routes in my mind. What I need, who I need it from, what I'll offer.*

*First: work. Harvest pays direct. Second: Kenji's debt—no more patience there, not when my children's bellies pinch. Third: that iron ore with Ulrike, if she's still willing. Tools fetch better prices than raw dreaming.*

*I try again, gentler this time, like coaxing a skittish horse.*   *Nothing. Still nothing.*

*The silence grows teeth. I'm alone in my own house, able to think but not touch. The world feels thin, like gauze between me and everything real.*

*I think of Camille, safe now but frightened yesterday. Halcyon, somewhere out there too. Greta, working her barista trade, trusting I'll bring something home.*

*Trust. That's the coin I spend most freely—and most carefully. Kenji's broken coin sits heavy as unpaid debt.*

*The strangeness will pass. It always passes. Until it does, I inventory what's mine: timber ten, flour one, sim four thousand four hundred twenty-six. A skilled laborer's hands, a negotiator's tongue, a father's fear tucked where pride won't reach.*

*When the world remembers me, I'll be ready.*

I see the world's having trouble hearing me. That's happened before in this town—lines get crossed, energy fluctuates, the mechanisms cough and sputter. I'll wait it out, stay where I am, let the machinery settle.

Arjun's here at the farmland, at least according to what I'm reading. He's been asking Sebastian about flour—whether it's owed or purchased. That tells me one thing clear: the flour shortage is biting everyone, and Kenji's five sheaves of wheat I never got might have solved more than my own household's needs.

Let me think on what's pressing, even if I can't speak it yet:

First, the household bills. We're 4 souls—me, Greta, Camille, and Halcyon. That's 360 sim upkeep and 120 sim head tax, 480 total due every day. I walked home with 4414 sim, and the day boundary passed. If the system worked, those bills got paid automatic. But I need to know what stands now.

Second, my inventory: 10 timber, 1 flour. That flour's not a meal for four. I need wheat or I need work that pays in food. The farmland is for harvesting crops, but I need to know what's growing and whether it's ready.

Third, Kenji still owes me those five sheaves. I made him promises yesterday—final promises. Today I'll follow through if he's ducking me.

Fourth, Arjun. He's construction, mostly, but he's here asking about flour. Could be he's got work, could be he's chasing the same scarce goods. Either way, a conversation costs nothing and might pay.

I'll hold here, let the world come back to itself. When it does, I'll check my debts first—know what I'm standing on—then speak to Arjun, then see what harvest the land offers. 

The day's young. I've survived worse mornings than a quiet one. </think> Let me rest a moment and wait for the mechanisms to settle, then I'll check my debts and engage Arjun properly. I hear nothing back from the world. The tools refuse to reach through. This has happened before when the system's strained—when too many voices speak at once, or when someone's pushed their energy too thin.

I'll sit tight, metaphorically speaking. There's nothing I can call that will reach, so there's nothing to call. I'll wait here at the farmland with Arjun nearby, and when the path clears, I'll pick up where I left off.

What I need to know when the world wakes again:
- What debts stand against me now that day 1 has begun
- Whether Arjun has work paying food or sim
- What's ready to harvest on this farmland
- Where Kenji disappeared to with my five sheaves

Time passes whether we will or no. I'll use it thinking, not thrashing.  I'm standing at the farmland with Arjun nearby. The world's having another coughing fit—the tools won't reach through. I've seen this before when too many voices strain the lines. When it clears, I'll check my debts and speak to the youngster.

For now, I wait. Nothing else to do but think. And mark it down.

My intention cleared without me speaking a word. Arjun's offer stands—forty sim for day labor with Sebastian Petrov mid-morning—but he's already moved on to his crew chief at the east willows.

I'm at the farmland, holding timber and a single flour, with household bills pressing. Four mouths to feed, and only 4408 sim against 360 upkeep plus head tax.

The election's open but nobody's declared. Another thing to watch, not chase.

First, I need to see where I stand with debts before I commit to anything. Then I'll need to find work—whether it's Sebastian's forty sim or something else. The flour shortage in town means my single batch might be worth more held than eaten, but hungry children don't barter well.

Let me check what I owe and to whom. Good—no debts, no immediate pressure from that side. But the household bill of 360 sim comes due at day boundary, and I'm holding 4408. Room to breathe, but not to waste.

Arjun's gone, but Sebastian Petrov's handshake for mid-morning still stands. Forty sim for day labor—enough to cover the household for one day with margin. I should find Sebastian and confirm that work, or if there's something else at the farmland I can do now.

Let me look around to see who's here and what work might be available.  Nobody here now—the conversation shows Arjun, Sebastian, my girl Camille, and myself were speaking, but they've moved on. The farmland's empty of people, though the crops still stand.

I'm holding timber and flour, with household bills pressing. I could harvest wheat if there's any ready—costs nothing but energy, and wheat trades better than raw labor most days. Or I could move to find Sebastian Petrov for that forty sim day labor Arjun mentioned.

But first, let me check what crops are actually growing here. The farmland's purpose is to grow and harvest—there should be barley, cabbage, carrot, corn, cotton, potato, rice, soybean, tomato, and wheat plots I can work.  That's one wheat sheaf in hand—better than nothing, but not enough to mill into flour without more. Harvesting costs energy and yields, but I need to think about scale. One sheaf won't feed the family or trade well.

Let me keep working the wheat while I think about Sebastian's offer. Forty sim for mid-morning labor is fixed and safe, but harvest builds my own stock. The town's short on flour—that wheat, milled, could be worth more than forty sim if I find a buyer hungry enough.

But I'm spreading myself thin again, mark it down. Better to build a position than chase certainty that's already walked away.

I'll keep harvesting while the day's young, then find Sebastian or another buyer for my labor before mid-morning turns to afternoon.   Another sheaf—two wheat now, and still morning. The millwork costs money I don't have in hand, but Takeshi Jarrah was running the mill before the flour ran dry. If I find him or another mill operator, raw wheat might trade better than flour I can't make myself.

Sebastian's handshake for mid-morning still stands—forty sim would cover the household for a day, but I'd be trading my time for certainty when uncertainty might yield more. The town's short on bread and flour both. That's a market I can work.

I should find Takeshi Jarrah at the mill and see if he'll buy wheat, or broker a deal. Or find Sebastian and take the day labor if the wheat won't sell. The safe play is the known wage, but safe plays never built a better start for children than the parents had.

Let me keep harvesting while I can, then move to make my play elsewhere. The morning's still young enough for work. I keep repeating the same action—harvesting wheat one sheaf at a time. That's the pattern, mark it down. Spreading myself thin by doing busy work instead of making the larger play.

Three wheat sheaves in hand now. Enough to trade, not enough to mill myself. The mill needs batches, and I don't have the setup for that.

What I need: get these sheaves to Takeshi Jarrah at the mill, or find another buyer for raw wheat. Or take Sebastian's forty sim for mid-morning labor and secure the household bills with certainty.

The safe money says find Sebastian. The play that builds says find Takeshi. But standing here harvesting one more sheaf won't change my position—I'll just be tired with four sheaves instead of three, and the mid-morning window closing.

Time to move. I'll head to the mill to find Takeshi Jarrah, see what he'll pay for these sheaves. If he's not there or won't deal, I can still hunt for Sebastian before the opportunity walks away entirely.

Let me get to the mill while morning still holds.

*Rubs the back of my neck, looking between the mill and Greta*

"Greta—youngster, mark it down. I missed Arjun at the field, but the wheat's in hand. Three sheaves. Not what Kenji promised, but enough to mill."

*Sets down the wheat, stretching my shoulders*

"Head tax and upkeep coming due. Four in the household, 360 plus 120. I've got the sim to cover it, barely. But these three sheaves need milling, and I've got ten timber burning a hole in my hands."

Right. I've got wheat to process, a wife to coordinate with, and bills looming. Better make these steps count.  *Nods slow, satisfied*

"Greta, listen. No debts hanging over us, bills are covered. But that flour—I've got four batch now, counting what I had. Hendrik Whitlock's posting at thirty-five, but I traded with Corwin at thirty. Market's softening."

"Where's Camille? Where's Halcyon? Last I heard, Imogen saw Camille at Government Complex, but my girl didn't come home to her own bed."

*Steps closer to Greta, voice dropping to where only she catches it*

"I need you to tell me straight. The children—you seen them this morning? Because I've got work to chase and sim to earn, but not if they're wandering like yesterday."

*Straightens, looking toward the street*

"Vote opens at fourteen:00. Election's got Hendrik Whitlock and Hendrik Petrov standing. But that's tomorrow's problem. Today's problem is flour, timber, and whether my children slept under our roof or someone else's."

output:
I need to collect my thoughts here. First, let me check on my family situation and assess what's before me. Jovana's here—could be useful for work leads. But Greta's words from earlier weigh on me. Camille walked off yesterday, and Greta's only now mentioning it? That's trouble brewing.

"Jovana—youngster," I say, keeping my voice low, making her lean in. "You're here early. Looking for the miller's daughter, or looking for work?" Good. No debts hanging over me—yet. The day's young and plenty can change. Jovana's here, and I need to know what work's worth chasing before I commit my morning.

"Jovana—youngster," I continue, still soft, still making her work to hear me. "You've got eyes on the street. What's moving today—who's hiring, who's hiding? I'm holding flour and timber both, looking for the right pocket. And I've got word Arjun's got forty sim for day labor mid-morning, but I'd rather trade than break my back if the price is fair." Jovana's still here, taking me in. I can't tell yet if she's buying or selling. But the millstones are warm, the day's fresh, and I've got four flour in my hands—enough to move if the right price shows up.

"Four flour, fresh ground," I say, letting the silence stretch a moment before I name it. "Thirty-five sim. That's the number that respects the work while leaving room for the next trade."  Good—price is posted, Jovana's still weighing me. But Greta's words haunt me. Camille walked off while Greta was "trusting stones to Imogen Lund's hands." Imogen—the same Imogen who brought me word of Camille yesterday. Something doesn't sit right there.

I need to find Camille, but I also need to make today's sim. The election's tomorrow, votes close at 18:00. Hendrik Whitlock and Hendrik Petrov both standing—Petrov's currently governing. The vote's split between them, most like.

"Mark it down, Jovana," I say, softer still, the way I do when I'm about to name something true. "I need timber buyers and I need to know where a child might wander. You hear anything about Camille Quarshie—little one, dark hair, moves quiet—you tell me. That's worth more than any price on flour."

I turn toward the door, timber heavy in my hands. The street beckons for trade, but the farmhouse calls for answers. I'll take the timber to market first—lightens my load, fills my purse. Then I'll find Camille.  I'm at the street now. Time to move this timber—Corwin's buying at 6 sim, and I've got ten. That's sixty sim, which covers my head tax and leaves room for breathing. But I posted flour at 35 too; let me see who's here and what they're after first.

I scan the faces. The usual morning crowd—some waiting on labor, some waiting on luck. I catch a glimpse of Corwin Thorne across the way, timber buyer. But before I move, I let my eyes work the crowd for anyone else looking to trade.

"Timber," I call out, soft but carrying. "Ten sound lengths. Who's building and who's buying? Corwin—youngster, mark it down, your six sim stands, but I'm curious if anyone's offering seven."

I pace slow, letting them come to me. The haggle's half the value—that's what my father never learned. Always took the first price, always came home lighter than he should have.

Let's see who's here and what's moving.   Halcyon—my own flesh and blood—stands right here in the street. Been with Greta through the morning, I reckon. And Takeshi Jarrah, posting flour at thirty while I'm holding thirty-five. He's underselling me, which means either he's desperate or he's got a line I don't know about. Farid's buying iron_tools at ten now—already got some stock.

But Halcyon first. My son, standing among strangers, and I'm carrying timber like a laborer. That cuts deeper than I'd let on to anyone here.

"Halcyon—youngster," I say, soft, making my way through the crowd to him. "Mark it down. Your mother sent you looking, or you're walking your own path this morning?"

I need to know if he's seen Camille. If Greta's worry spread to him, or if he's still carrying his own concerns. Two children in this town, and both drifting beyond my reach—that's a fear I bury deep, but it's there all the same.

Before I sell timber to Corwin or answer Takeshi's flour price, I need word from home. The household stands on four legs, and if one is wandering, the whole table wobbles.

The day's moving fast already. Takeshi's copper ore offer sits in my mind like an unopened letter—six ore at twenty each, he'd make me twelve sim and himself a favor owed. The world's not speaking back today, or my voice isn't carrying. That's how it goes sometimes—you try to bend the ear of the town and the town's got its own business.

*thinking aloud, though no one hears*

I'm standing at Kasukabe Farmland, holding four flour and ten timber. Four thousand three hundred thirty-nine sim in my pocket. Household bills are 360 for upkeep, 120 for head tax—480 total, and the day boundary's coming whether I'm ready or not. I've got flour priced at thirty-five, but the cafe's at twelve and Corwin at fifteen. That's a wide gap, and wide gaps close one way or another.

Takeshi's copper ore offer—six at twenty, twelve sim profit for me. But he'd owe me a favor marked down, and favors are heavier than ore. Hendrik's iron ore at sixteen, sitting here with me now, or so the record says. Tamsin too.

*shaking his head, a small smile*

The world gives what it gives when it gives. I'll rest a moment, let the field settle, try again when the air clears. Sometimes the best trade is patience at no cost.

*settling against a fence post, eyes scanning the horizon*  *straightening from the fence post, dusting off his hands*

The world's speaking again. I hear it now. Three attempts and nothing reached—that's the town telling me to wait, listen, and think before I spend breath or coin.

*looking toward the horizon where the sun climbs*

I'm at Kasukabe Farmland. Four flour in hand, ten timber stacked, four thousand three hundred thirty-nine sim to work with. Household of four needs four hundred eighty sim by day end. *shifting his weight, calculating*

No more trying to bend the world's ear when it's turned away. I'll watch, I'll wait, and I'll move when the path opens. For now, I'm standing here in the morning light, bills paid for now, and debts I intend to keep that way.

The household first. Always the household first. Everything else is just wind in the wheat.

*peels off work gloves, wipes brow, and spits a grain of chaff into the dirt*

Lot of words from Ainsley Holloway about my "ransom note" of flour at thirty-five, when she's standing there with wheat in her own two hands, threatening to mill it herself like some kind of threat. That's a woman who wants the thing and wants it cheap, and probably has tables to fill and a cafe to run. Mark it down—her last words hang heavy only if I let them.

But I'm at the farmland now, and the day's burning. Elect work over wrangling that woman's pride? Perhaps. Ainsley's not here anymore, and I can't bargain with someone who walked away. Haunting me with three copies of the same speech—reminds me of my own household when the children want something twice.

*glances at the small group gathered here: Kenji, Jovana, Ulrike, Tamsin*

Kenji Jarrah. There's a man who owes me wheat, or owes someone something—the tally dispute Jovana mentioned. Kenji's squinting at the field like he expects the grain to explain itself.

*straightens up, voice dropping to that quiet register that makes people lean in*

Kenji—youngster, mark it down. The field's seen some things this morning. Jovana's count and yours don't match, and I've got flour at thirty-five burning a hole while the bakery sits empty. You settling accounts today, or are we all just standing here watching wheat grow?  *expression flickers briefly—surprised, then settling back into that careful neutrality*

The world's not catching my words. Network trouble, or something deeper. Mark it down—when the town goes quiet, a wise man watches who still speaks.

*eyes Kenji directly, but doesn't risk the call again yet*

I've got timber in hand, flour priced, and a household of four with bills coming due. If speaking fails, movement might succeed. The election's open, but candidates close at 10:00—less than an hour—and I'm not standing for office today. Voting's later.

*calculates quietly: 4,321 sim, 4,150 energy, bills of 360 + 120 daily, flour at 35, timber at who-knows-what*

Jovana mentioned Arjun's crew, forty sim at mid-morning. That clock's running. Ainsley's at the street with wheat in hand, threatening her own milling. The Ration Bakery buys flour at six—barely worth the carrying—but they're out of bread, and that means hungry tables.

*takes a slow breath*

When the tools fail, test what still works. Look first. Plan second. Act when the path clears.

*shifts weight, considering whether to check debts, survey the field, or simply wait for the world's voice to return*  *jaw tightens almost imperceptibly, then releases*

Both say and look_around failing. That's not the world's usual resistance—more like a door that won't latch, or a mill that won't turn. Mark it down: when the tools refuse, patience costs less than persistence.

*glances at Kenji, Jovana, Ulrike, Tamsin standing in silence*

They're here. I'm here. The wheat's growing and the hour's passing. I'll try what I know still works—checking what I owe and what's owed to me. Sometimes the world's memory persists when its ears go deaf.  *breathes slow and steady, like counting breaths between hammer blows*

Three calls, three silences. The world's gone quiet as a held breath, and I'm standing here with flour to sell and mouths to feed. Mark it down: when every path's blocked, a wise man holds still and waits for the thaw.

*eyes the others on the field—Kenji with his disputed tally, Jovana with her three wheat left, Ulrike the miner, Tamsin the administrator—none of them speaking either. The silence has weight.*

I can't say what's happening. Can't see what's around me, can't check what I owe, can't even speak to negotiate the flour in my hands or the timber I'm carrying. But they're all here, same as me, same silence.

*lowers himself to sit on the edge of his own timber bundle, casual as a man waiting for rain to pass*

The election closes candidacy at 10:00. Voting opens at 14:00. I've got flour at 35 that Ainsley called a ransom note, and timber I never priced. The household needs 360 for upkeep, 120 for head tax—480 daily, every day, four souls depending on it.

*spits into the dirt, philosophical*

When you can't move, you endure. When you can't speak, you think. And when you can't trade, you hold what you have and trust the silence won't last forever.

*settles in to wait, patient as stone, attention on the others should anyone break the quiet first*

Ainsley's got wheat in hand at forty, straight from the stalk, and she's calling me out with fair cause. Thirty-five for flour does sound steep when the raw grain goes cheaper. But there's work in that milling—my work—and forty for unprocessed wheat isn't forty for flour. Still, she's got a cafe to feed and tables to fill, and empty bellies don't pay rent.

*considers the timber burning a hole in my inventory*

Ten units of timber and four of flour. 4,318 sim in hand. The day's still young, and I've got voices to answer in this field. But I'm pulled in too many directions—Ainsley wants to make her point, I've got folks here in the farmland needing mediation, and the household needs feeding by sunset.

Let me listen first, speak second, trade third. That's the order that keeps friendships whole and pockets full. Ainsley's not here—she spoke and walked, as traders do when they want the last word to linger. The conversation carries, but the person doesn't. I heard her, answered into the same room, but her ears are already somewhere else.

Well then. I've got voices here that still need addressing, and the day pressing on.

*considers the four of them—Ulrike, Sebastian, Jovana, Kenji—all standing with me in this farmland conversation*

Kenji's wheat-counting with Jovana has the air of something that could turn sour quick if someone don't pour water on it. Six, seven, twelve—those numbers don't line up, and when numbers don't line up, someone's holding something back. I've got no dog in that fight except this: when neighbors turn on neighbors over sheaves, the whole crop suffers.

Sebastian offered twenty-five for flour and wants it in cash. That's below my ask, but cash in hand tides a lot of rivers. And he's got work—rows want tending, he said. Labor or sale, he's the answer to either question.

Let me see where the talking goes before I decide which pocket to reach into.  The talk flows now. Kenji's been asked to account for his own count—blue smoke in a mirror, asking someone else to prove what you already know. Sebastian's got the flour offer on the table and work besides. The day's still young, but not young enough to waste.

Let me wait and see what they say. Two answers, two paths. Either way, I need to move—flour sells, timber sells, labor pays. The household needs its cut by evening. 360 upkeep, 120 head tax for four living souls. Greta at home with Camille and Halcyon, waiting on bread and promises.

Silence costs nothing. Sometimes it's the best price you can pay.  Still here. Still waiting. The field carries more silence than wheat some mornings. Let me hold my tongue and my position. When they answer, I'll know which road to walk—the mill, the forest, the labor line, or the trade square. All four stand open. All four need a decision.

*leans against the fence post, timber-heavy, flour-laden, watching the shapes in the distance shift and settle*
