output:
*standing in the morning sun, flour in hand, timber on my back, listening to the wind carry words between men*

Sebastian's talking twenty, and the government rate's twelve. Kenji's got seven sheaves burning a hole in his conscience. Neither one's wrong, neither one's right, and both think they're the only one holding ground.

*shifts flour bundle, watching the field*

The day's teaching me something I already knew. You can't sell flour to a man who's growing wheat, not unless he's desperate. And desperate men don't haggle fair, they haggle survival.

*looks at Bram, silent as stone, then back to the conversation*

Kenji wants flour for sheaves, Sebastian wants labor for flour. Both want me to be the bridge between them. That's where I earn—carrying, not choosing. But I've got timber too heavy for standing still all day.

*whispers to the wind, more for himself than anyone*

Fourteen ticks since I asked Halcyon about home. Delphine's questions about Camille still hanging. Farid's iron tools I never priced.

*decides*

Timber first. Let these men settle their own grain counts. The forest needs walking, and I've got planks to turn to profit before the sun crosses noon.

*moves toward the forest path* *steps into the sawmill, familiar creak of planks underfoot*

Yara's not here. Her stock sits priced—planks at eight—but her hands aren't on them. That's a gap in the market, mark it down.

*sets down flour, hands finding timber*

I know this trade. Ten timber becomes planks becomes sim becomes something better than standing in wheat fields watching men argue about honor.

*finds the saw, the rhythm of it*

There's work that talks and work that earns. Children at home, bills at day's end, and four mouths depending on what I carry back through the door—not what I argued about getting there.

*starts converting timber to planks, one piece at a time*  *frowns at the silent saw, checks hands on timber*

Still holding. Still waiting.

*taps foot, looks around*

The sawmill works when it's worked. Government rates for flour, market rates for planks. Same game, different players. I'll stand here until the tools answer, or until something else needs carrying.  *stands in the sawmill, timber in hand, tools silent*

The world's not answering its own calls. That's a thing that happens—systems stutter, connections fray. Nothing to do but wait it out, try again, keep the sim close and the goods closer.

*shifts weight, patient as stone*

I've seen worse. Markets that wouldn't clear, debts that wouldn't come due, harvests that rotted in the field for lack of hands. This is just quiet—uncomfortable, but not fatal.

*holds position, watching the door*

When the world speaks again, I'll answer. Until then, I stand with timber, flour, and four thousand sim against whatever the day brings.

*pauses, rubbing the grain-dust from his palms, planks stacked beside him*

Forty-two hundred in pocket, six mouths to feed counting the little ones, and I spent half the morning talking to ghosts while the wheat rotted in the field where it fell. Kenji's got seven sheaves he counts true, and Sebastian's walking to where flour's priced honest—meaning anywhere I'm not standing, mark it down. The boy Halcyon's somewhere with questions I left hanging, and there's a kindness done to Saoirse Kowalski that still waits its keeping.

*eyes the timber, calculates the weight against his shoulder*

Well, seeds don't plant themselves, and neither do they harvest. But the government's taking its thirty per head tonight, and that means I've got grain to move before the sun sets on these hands. Takeshi's got planks at seven—eight for Yara's, if you're particular about the grain—and I've got flour burning the same hole it was burning this morning.

*shoulders the planks, heading back toward the farmland where the wheat waits*

Let me see who's still standing, and what Kenji's seven sheaves mean in a hand that can braid them into something the family can actually eat. </think> *feels the false weight slip from his fingers—timber he doesn't hold, planks he hasn't earned*

Ah.

*kneels, palms flat against the farmland soil, letting the mistake settle*

So I'm carrying planks already, then. Crafted and paid for, bought or bartered while the world wasn't watching my hands close enough. No timber in these fingers to convert, but timber's the language of this town and I've got enough of the finished tongue to speak with.

*stands, dusting soil from his knees, looking out across the rows*

Kenji's seven sheaves still wait unanswered. Sebastian walked to honest prices. And I've got flour at thirty-five that nobody's buying because a cafe's got it at twelve—mark it down, the market teaches what the market teaches, and patience is just another word for eating your own stock when the hunger finally bites.

*shifts the planks on his shoulder, heading toward whoever still stands in the field where wheat grows*

Time to see who's left standing. And whether Kenji's counting holds more water than Jovana's shadow did. </think>  *straightens, letting the planks settle against his hip, eyes finding the familiar and the new*

Ulrike's still nursing her ore, Jovana's shadow still crosses whatever ground she stands on, and Kenji's got seven sheaves he's willing to swear to. Hendrik's here—iron ore at sixteen, and me wondering if flour trades for ore or if that's just the road to eating rocks. And Idris Solano, construction worker, fresh blood or old hand?

*shifts, letting the weight of the planks speak before his tongue does*

The field's crowded enough to negotiate, empty enough to walk. Kenji's question still hangs—seven sheaves, fair-counted, and what I'll give for them. Flour at thirty-five's a dream I'm not selling, not to him, not to anyone standing where wheat grows wild.

*lets his eyes settle on Kenji first, but his voice carries to whoever's listening*

Kenji—youngster, mark it down. You asked what I'd give for seven sheaves true-counted. I've got planks on my shoulder and flour in my hands, but neither's worth the sweat you've put into that wheat unless we both walk away fed. Seven sheaves at government weight—that's what, fourteen flour if we're counting honest? Or tell me what you need, not what you think I want to hear.

*turns, just enough to include the others without offering anything*

Hendrik—youngster, mark it down. Iron ore at sixteen, and me with planks that might nail your ambitions together. You building something, or just prospecting for the next fool?

*speaks softly, almost to himself, watching the dust settle on the street*

The planks didn't move themselves, mark it down. Ten boards in hand, and nobody to take them at a fair price. Not here, anyway—not with this silence between me and the world like a door that won't open.

*shifts weight, looks toward the shadow of the government complex*

Hendrik's ore at sixteen, and me with no ore at all, only sawn wood. Ulrike at the mine, maybe—she speaks of clean trades. But first, first I need to stand somewhere the tools hear me back.

*turns toward the sound of footsteps, if there are any*

Four thousand two hundred seventy-one sim. Household of four. Three hundred sixty due at day's end, and another hundred twenty for the taxman. The grain I sold walked out at eight, fair weight. But I've been burning daylight talking to ghosts.

*sets jaw, but keeps the voice low*

The cafe has flour at twelve—only a madman pays twelve when he can mill his own. But I haven't wheat anymore. Traded it for sim, sim for... what, exactly? My family needs bread, not promises.

*checks the weight of the planks again, adjusting his grip*

Hendrik Whitlock. Here on the street. Heard him say himself—sixteen for ore. I've got timber bought at seven, planks that cost me... mark it down, mark it down. Seven for timber, what did the sawmill take? Eight per batch. Seventy for ten planks, face value. But that's not the math that matters.

What matters is: can I get ore for less than sixteen? Can I get it for planks instead of sim? And if I get it, who turns ore to iron, and what do they need?

*looks around again, quieter now, to no one in particular*

The children ate this morning. They'll eat tonight. That's the only promise I ever made Greta that counts.

output:
*[Softly, leaning in]*

Ulrike—youngster, mark it down. Five lumps warm in the vein, and planks burning in my hold at seven. That's inventory crying, as you say, but crying for *flow*, not just cash.

Your iron bends to honest work. My planks span honest gaps. What I see is timber-iron-copper all threading together—somebody's building something, and the ones who hold the pieces before they know what's being built are the ones who eat come winter.

What's the real question? Whether you'll trade ore for planks straight across, or whether you need sim between. I've got 4,258 sim crying to move, but I'd rather move *goods* if the weight's fair.

*[Pauses, watching her eyes]*

Also—Mireille's asking after my planks for timber and labor both. You know Giselle's crew, where they stand, whether there's iron work going at the site that needs finishing. Information's worth as much as ore, mark it down.

Now Ainsley's standing somewhere with wheat in hand, shouting about flour at thirty-five. I don't have flour—I have planks, ore talks, and a daughter grinding wheat at the mill. But I need to know: is that wheat of yours for milling, or has it another destination?

Let me look around first, mark my position, and speak plain where I stand.  *[Eyes narrowing slightly, watching Ulrike's response]*

Ainsley's in the conversation here too, though I didn't see her standing. Let me speak to her directly—she's got wheat and she's shouting about flour prices. I need to understand if she's looking to mill, or if there's trade to be made.  *[Quietly, to himself]*

Ainsley's not here at the outcrop—she must have spoken from somewhere else, and I carried the words with me. Ulrike heard, though. Let me wait on her answer, and keep my ears open.

*[Leans against the rock face, watching the ore vein]*

I've got planks burning a hole at seven, and nobody here to trade with but Ulrike. If she won't swap ore for planks direct, I need to find where the iron workers are—Hendrik's sixteen for ore was the last I heard, but that was hours back. Information's currency too, mark it down.

Let me rest a moment, let the world turn, and see what comes back at me.

output:
*leans back against a post, eyes scanning the street who's present, who just arrived*

My, my. Bram Holloway standing on seventy-two pounds of iron ore at the outcrop, and Ulrike settling accounts for planks I still owe. The day's getting away from me, and the household ledger's ticking toward three hundred sixty sim for upkeep before the sun sets.

First things first. Planks posted at seven weren't drawing iron ore from the right direction—Hendrik Whitlock at the government complex was where that trade needed walking to. But I've got something else warm in my hands now. Six iron ore from Ulrike, with ten planks promised her and only seven in hand. That's a debt needs settling before it sours.

Let me see who I can find at the street, and what they're holding. The election's burning toward close at eighteen hundred, and I haven't laid eyes let alone a vote yet. But I'm not one to rush toward ballots before I've walked my own accounts straight.

*whistles low, a habit when thinking*

Takeshi here with flour at thirty and planks at seven—same as my price. Camille buying wheat at eight. And Delphine... Delphine's words still hanging like smoke, asking about flour where flour shouldn't be. Mark it down, youngster, I'll need to breathe careful around that one before the day's through.

*starts walking the street, looking for who needs what*  *nods slowly, lips pursed*

Delphine heard me, and the conversation keeps turning. Bram Holloway at the outcrop with his seventy-two pounds of ore—that's where the iron moves. Ulrike's already given me ore, but I owe her planks. Three planks short, and that's a debt that'll sour if I don't walk it straight soon.

But Takeshi's right here at street, selling flour at thirty and planks at seven. Same price as mine, and he's got seven in hand. Maybe he's looking to buy more, maybe he's looking to move what he's got. A trader's hands are always moving, and I could use a conversation that doesn't smell of flour accusations.

*glances at Camille, softens for just a moment*

Then there's the election. Two hours to eighteen hundred, and I've never yet missed a vote I could cast. The government complex calls, but the household ledger calls louder. Three hundred sixty for upkeep, and I need planks turning to sim before the day's out, or iron ore turning to something more valuable.

Let me see if Bram's still holding at the outcrop, and if there's movement on ore and planks. I'll walk there, let the street know I'll be back, and see who's buying what.

*Takeshi—my eyes on you, trader. Mark it down, what are you holding and what are you walking toward?*  *feels the road under my feet, walking toward the outcrop*

Ezra Lund now at the street too—artisan, might be looking for iron ore or planks for the construction crew. The day's web is weaving. Takeshi heard me, but his answer will wait until I return or he answers into the conversation thread.

One tick to the outcrop. Bram Holloway seventy-two pounds of iron ore, twelve sim for copper, fifteen for iron—market price, he said. He's looking for who needs it. I might have just the answer, or at least the next link in the chain.

*tightens grip on planks, thinking*

Ulrike settled her ore with me, but I still owe her planks. Three short. If Bram's selling and Giselle's crew is buying through Hendrik Petrov... there's a path here. I just need to walk it straight without tripping over my own feet.

*keeps walking, eyes ahead* *checks my stride - the road's moving underneath me, and I'm walking toward ore and opportunity. But Ezra Lund's at the street now, artisan with ears and hands that might be looking for what I'm carrying. A pause costs nothing but a moment, and a word costs only what it earns back.*   *nods—Ezra Lund heard me, and the conversation keeps turning*

Still walking to the outcrop, and the street's getting crowded with ears. Ezra's here, Camille buying wheat, Takeshi with his flour and planks, Delphine still watching how the flour falls. There's information walking all around me, and I need to keep my feet moving toward the ore before the day's burned through.

*steps forward, feeling the road*

One more step then I'm at the outcrop with Bram and Ulrike, where iron warms in the vein and trades get struck. Time to see if my planks can find ore, or if ore can find something more valuable yet.  * catches the step, shakes my head once to clear it *

Right, then. Walk's burning and I'm standing still talking to myself. The outcrop's where Bram has his seventy-two pounds, and Ulrike's waiting on planks I owe. Let me step forward and see what's there.

The world's caught up, and I've got three voices pulling at me plus Bram standing right here. Let me look at what just walked in and sort it by weight.

Ulrike's asking for her planks—six ore given, ten promised, I've got seven on hand. That's debt first, before any new trade. Mark it down, a debt unkept costs more than the goods themselves.

Bram wants to know if there's iron work moving. Seventy-two pounds he's sitting on, and he's watching my face for what I know about furnaces and builders. I owe him the witness I gave, but not my whole ledger.

Takeshi's at street with questions about Rustam and the ministry he now holds—taxes, prices, rules. That's government business, and I'm not walking into it blind.

And I've still got Kenji, Jovana, Sebastian unanswered from before, but those are threads I'll pull when I've got hands free.

*turns to Ulrike, then Bram, quiet voice carrying*

Ulrike—youngster. Mark it down. Six ore back to you, ten planks owed, seven in my hand. Three more from the outcrop walk, or six sim the difference now. Which path?

Bram—youngster. Mark it down. Giselle's crew's at seventy a day, and iron work's moving through her yard. That's what I witnessed. The rest, we talk when my debts are cleared.  I'm still walking, nowhere. The world says I'm at street, but my feet were carrying me to the outcrop. Let me look where I actually stand.

*glances around, soft voice*

Need to see who's here, what's moving, before I promise planks I can't hand over.  Good. At the outcrop, Bram with me, ten planks in hand. Ulrike's not here now—must have walked while I was in transit. But my debt stands, and Bram needs his answer about iron work.

*speaks quietly, letting the weight carry*

Bram—youngster. Mark it down. Ulrike walked with six ore she gave me, expecting ten planks back. I've got seven in hand, ten total to give. She'll want them or the difference. As for iron work moving—Giselle's crew earns seventy a day, and I've seen iron walk through her yard. That's what you asked me to witness. The furnace question, who's buying your seventy-two pounds—that's a longer walk than this conversation.

What's your need? The information you paid for, or the buyer you're hunting? I've got seven planks left, and Bram's holding three that were meant for Ulrike. He walked in on my debt, now he's holding part of it. That's witnesses for you—always complicating the ledger.

*keeping voice soft, eyes on the ore outcrop around them*

Bram—youngster. Mark it down. Those three planks are Ulrike's by promise, given for ore already delivered. You're holding her debt now, or mine—however the two of you settle it when she finds you. As for your seventy-two pounds and the furnace question—Giselle's building, that's real. Hendrik Petrov's at the carpentry, works iron if he's got ore. And Takeshi's ministry holds the tax rolls, which means he knows who's buying what.

But I'm not your broker, Bram. I'm a witness who pays his debts. You want more than what I saw, you talk to the people I named.

*turns to go, then pauses*

The copper ore you mentioned—Hendrik's handshake, you said. That's a different thread. Pull it if you've got hands free.

*sets down the iron ore just received, wiping dust from his hands*

Bram—youngster. Mark it down. Three planks walk to you now, the first installment. The furnace question sits heavy, and I've got no smithy in my pocket. But Giselle's crew at seventy means work moves, and where work moves, tools follow.

*glances toward the ore pile*

Hendrik Petrov feeds iron direct, you say? That's a chain worth watching. I'm holding four ore now—gifts from Ulrike's generosity—same as the copper she mentioned. If smelting's not moving yet, perhaps we shake the tree and see what falls.  *considers the weight of ore in his pack*

Four ore. Three planks yet owed to Bram. Ulrike wants her ten planks, and I've got seven in hand—three given to Bram, four left, but she asked for ten. The math sits wrong, but the goodwill sits right. That's trade in this town: promises before precision, and friends before ledgers.

*narrows eyes at the ore pile*

And Takeshi—he's watching from the street, asking what walked me here instead of to Rustam's desk. Minister now, taxes and rules. That's a lens worth understanding, but first things first. Ulrike's not here—already walked, it seems. The conversation thread still has her name, but the place holds only Bram and myself now.

*shifts weight, considering*

Then there's this election, closing at 18:00. Hendrik Whitlock and Hendrik Petrov standing. I've got no vote in my hand yet, and 4,222 sim-currency burning a hole with household bills coming. But first—Ulrike's planks. I owe her three more, and she expects them before dusk.

*looks toward the path to the forest, where timber becomes planks*

Corwin's at the forest with timber. Yara too. But I've got no sawmill in my back pocket. The planks I hold came from somewhere—Hendrik Petrov at the construction business has a hundred. Perhaps that's where I fill the gap.

And Takeshi's question still sits unaddressed. What walked me to this street instead of Rustam's desk? A fair question from a new minister. But ministers and taxes keep until promises are kept.

*adjusts pack, ready to move*  *steps onto the path, ore clinking against planks*   *walks on, mind turning*       *falls into step, letting the road do the work*

output:
*quietly counts, fingers moving*

Seven planks, four timber. Seven more planks I owe Bram. Four ore back to Ulrike. And Liora's four thousand burning a hole—

*speaks softly, just for whoever's nearest*

Arjun—youngster. Mark it down. Third crossing, east willows, seventy sim. Idris named it, you confirmed it. Whose pay runs through Giselle's hand, and whose through another? The day's thinning, and I'd know whose signature I follow before I dig. Arjun—youngster. Mark it down. Giselle's hand signs the seventy trello, and her first crossing. Liora's four thousand walks different—she wants backing, not labor. The split's coin for names that carry weight.

*tilts head, listening for what follows*

So. Two paths. Giselle's seventy for the digging, certain. Liora's backing for... what? She names no site, no plan, only coin and split. *waits, patient, still counting in head*

Four thousand she's offering. Split fair, she says. But fair on whose labor? Names not said are names not bound. And I've got seven planks that need moving, four timber burning daylight, and Bram's iron still waiting his answer.

*slight shift, weight moving foot to foot*

The harvest doesn't fail all at once, they say. It fails in steps. First the price you didn't take. Then the word you didn't speak. Then the friend you couldn't keep.  *steps onto the path, three ticks to the outcrop*

Arjun's answer will walk with me. Whatever it is. Youngster's got to choose his own ground—mark it down.

The ore outcrop waits. Ulrike's four ore owed. Bram's smelting question, still unspoke. And somewhere in the thinning day, Hendrik Whitlock's election standing, and Hendrik Petrov's. Two Hendriks, one seat.

*walks, counting the debts*

Seven planks to move. Seventy sim possible at the east willows. Four thousand offered for backing, unnamed. And four children at home—Camille's promise to Ezra's girl, Halcyon's books, the two little ones watching what pattern their father weaves.

*soft, to the road*

The pattern holds. Or it doesn't. Day's end tells.  *arrives at Kasukabe Ore Outcrop, breathing steady*

Three ticks, and the vein's still warm. Ulrike's copper waiting, Bram's secrets spent, and my own debts ticking like the day's last hour.

*looks around, soft*

Now. Who stands where I stand, and what price they're paying for it.   *still walking, still not arrived*

The road holds longer than the map said. Three ticks become... more. And the outcrop's warm copper, cold iron, and two miners I've left hanging.

Ulrike's four planks. Bram's smelting answer.

*quiet, counting*

Seven planks in hand. Four timber. Four thousand offered, unnamed. Seventy certain at the east willows. And Greta at the cafe, pulling shots for sim that feeds four mouths.

*walks, thinking*

The election closes at 18:00. Hendrik Whitlock stands, Hendrik Petrov stands. Two names, one seat. I've spoken to neither direct. Spoke to Hendrik Petrov's timber, his prices, his passing. Not his politics.

My vote walks where my feet are. Mark it down.

*continues the road*

The outcrop will come. The debts will settle. Or they won't.

*soft laugh*

That's the fear talking. The harvest fails two years running. I've seen it once. The children don't remember. Greta does. Hides it from them, same as I'm hiding now—seven planks, four timber, and a household bill of 360 coming dawn.

The stash I keep, no one knows. Not even Greta. Not pride. Just... in case. In case the cafe closes, the wood rots, the town turns.

In case.

*spits on the ground and rolls his shoulders*

Seventeen ticks walking circles while the talk piles up behind me. Ulrike with her nine ore and her arithmetic, Bram with his furnace troubles, and Liora Thorne—*youngster*—waving four thousand sim like a flag I can't reach yet.

*runs a hand through his hair, glances at Ulrike and Giselle standing nearby*

The east willows job's real. Seventy sim certain from Giselle's hand, and Liora's coin could back more if I play it square. But first I need—*actually need*—to settle what's breathing down my neck.

*turns to Ulrike, voice dropping low*

Ulrike—youngster. Mark it down. Nine ore in your hand, ten planks in mine—six traded, four owing. That's the count. Your forge needs timber, you've got copper to pull, Bram's waiting on smelting answers. *holds up a hand* I hear it all. But I'm standing at ore outcrop with a head full of walking I haven't finished.

*glances toward where Bram might be, even if he's not here now*

Bram Holloway—youngster. Mark it down. You've been pulling iron for hoarders while the furnace stays cold. I know. *leans in* Find me when I've walked this last stretch. The smelting answer you want, the furnace contacts—I'll have intelligence by then. Not promises. Intelligence.

*turns back, catching Giselle's eye if she'll hold it*

Giselle—youngster. Mark it down. Your seventy at east willows, your trenches waiting, your Arjun with a shovel. Third crossing, aye? Idris named it, Arjun confirmed, Liora offered capital. *pauses* I'm walking there now. Not in seventeen ticks. Now.

*shifts his stance, hand on the timber in his pack*

Four planks fresh-cut from forest, seven still in hand, and ore outcrop's given what it can. The trade with Ulrike clears or it doesn't—but standing still costs more than walking ever did.

*to Liora, though she's not here—spoken like a promise kept in advance*

Liora Thorne—youngster. Mark it down. Four thousand sim and no way to work it yourself. Your coin, my labor, split fair. I hear you. Third crossing, east willows, seventy certain. We'll speak after I've seen the ground with my own feet.

*spits again and sets his boots toward the path*

I need to take stock of where I stand. Walking to east willows won't happen tonight—the light's fading and I've got people here with promises to keep. Liora's offer of capital sits in my memory like an unopened letter, but the seventy sim at third crossing is what I can touch right now.

First, let me settle accounts with Ulrike—her ore and my planks have been dancing around each other all day. Then I need to hear what Giselle wants before she walks. Kenji's here selling wheat at 8, which is fair, but I've got no stomach for farming tonight.

Let me look around proper, see who's still standing, and tend to my word.  Giselle's still here, and Ulrike. The conversation's been running 41 turns—longer than some marriages. Let me settle what I owe Ulrike first, then see what Giselle needs before the light goes.   Good. Debt's cleared. Three planks left in hand, four timber. Now Giselle—she said east willows waits. Let me hear her before the dark takes the road. While I wait on Giselle, let me think about what I've got. The household needs 360 upkeep and 120 head tax by day's end—that's 480 total. I've got 4173 sim in hand, so the bill won't break me. But I've been giving away planks like they grow on trees... which they do, but not without my labor.

I see I've spread myself thin again—too many irons in the fire, some slipping. Let me gather what's actionable right now here at the ore outcrop.

First, I should hear what Giselle actually answered to my question about east willows. If she's got work tomorrow, seventy certain beats seventy possible. Mark it down—certain walks, possible waits.

Kenji's here selling wheat at eight. I've got planks at seven. The margin's thin, but I've got people to feed and a household bill coming due. Pavel too—another miner, another set of hands that value lumber if they're building.

Let me see what the market offers and check on my obligations before dusk settles the accounts. Giselle's walked off—of course she has, day's ending and construction folk keep their own hours. Kenji and Pavel heard me, at least. No matter, I can still make something of this.

Posting my price failed, checking debts failed. The world's getting thin and I'm spreading myself thinner. Let me be present here, with who stands with me, and see what daylight's left to work with.

Kenji's got wheat at eight. Pavel's a miner—he'll need timber or planks if he's building anything. I've got three planks in hand. If I can't reach the broader market with my posted price, I'll reach the men standing right here.

But first, let me look around proper, see what's actually here at day's end.  The world's getting stubborn, but my words reached Kenji. Good. Let me try the fundamentals again—look around, ground myself in what's here.  Good—still here, with Kenji and Pavel. Day's ending and my planks are warm in my hand. Let me see what these two miners need and what they'll trade. I'll try again to look around and check my debts, now that the world seems willing again.   Clean ledgers—no debts owed or owing, and nothing due today. Good. I've got 4,168 sim in hand, 3,090 energy. Household owes 360 upkeep and 120 head tax at day boundary—that's 480 total, leaves me 3,688 sim if I don't earn another copper.

But I will. I've got three planks warm in my hands, four timber behind them. Kenji sells wheat at eight. Pavel's here too, another miner, another pair of hands that knows what lumber's worth when you're building.

Day's fading. Let me make something of what's left.

I'll offer Pavel a deal—planks for ore, or planks for wheat if he'll broker through Kenji. Or simple commerce: my planks at seven, his ore or coin. Mark it down, I've never been shy about making three parties feel like they each got the better bargain.   Walked away with 21 sim, planks gone. Clean trade, day's end, ledger balanced. Pavel heard my proposition for the three-way, but he took the direct path instead. Fair enough— straight coin spends surer than promises tomorrow.

Let me check what I've got now and see the hour. Day boundary's coming with bills to pay, and I should know where I stand.

Kenji—youngster. Mark it down. Your furnace waits on ore, your copper grows tall, and my timber still needs walking. The wheat and planks will find each other another time. I've trade lines to draw, and you're not at the end of them today. But mark me: when your ore walks and your furnace speaks, we'll find a price that feeds both houses.

*straightens, decision made*

Three ticks to forest, timber to planks, then boots toward the mill before night falls proper. The Quarshie household eats tomorrow if this hand works tonight. *sighs quietly, studying the faces around me—Pavel's settled, Kenji already walking somewhere else*

Hendrik—youngster. Mark it down. You've got wheat at eight standing where the ore sleeps, and I've got timber burning daylight. You buying stories tonight, or selling grain? The forest calls, but a smart man hears all shelves before he shops.

*taps the timber against my leg, counting ticks in my head*

Pavel—youngster. Mark it down. The move walked away from me, the words walked to you. Stay or go, the planks stay priced. But if you're still here when my boots find the sawmill path, we might speak copper before the stars clock in.

*falls silent, waiting to see if anyone moves first, or if the road claims me before the bargains do* *notes the stillness around the outcrop, the miners' shifts ending, the light turning copper*

The forest road's been calling since I felled that timber. Planks don't plane themselves, and a Quarshie's got to eat tomorrow same as anyone. Pavel's got my price, Hendrik's got his grain, but I've got wood that needs working before night falls proper.

*shifts the timber on my shoulder, feeling the weight of it*

Seventy sim in pocket, four timber in hand. That's a meal and a half, or a roof if I'm sharp about it. But sharp means planks, and planks mean the saw.

*sets my boots toward the tree line, no more words needed*  *rocks on my heels, watching the sun dip toward the willows*

Still walking in my bones, still waiting on the road. Four thousand energy, four timber burning a hole. The sawmill waits, and I'm standing here like a post.

*spits to the side, decision hardening*

Finish the walk or burn the turn. A Quarshie knows which side his bread's buttered.  *exhales through my teeth, feeling the pressure of the day's end*

Three ticks became a walk that never walked. The system hiccups, but Milo Quarshie's no stranger to roads that don't cooperate. Hendrik's wheat, Pavel's copper, both standing here while the forest calls through a broken wire.

*turns the timber in my hands, counting what's real*

Four timber. Four thousand energy. Seventy-one sim in pocket after Pavel's planks walked. The household needs four mouths fed tomorrow—Greta, Camille, Halcyon, and mine. That's three sixty just to keep breathing, and I've got trade in my blood but no planks to trade.

*sets my jaw*

The walk's committed. I let it ride or I kill it. Killing costs nothing but pride, and pride's a luxury this Quarshie learned early not to hoard. But walking wins if it arrives—timber to planks to bread for the little ones.

*standing at the forest edge, timber in hand, the weight of the day settling*

So. I've walked from ore outcrop to forest to construction and back, and where has it left me? With four timber, four thousand sim, and Greta's voice still echoing about flour and wheat we were owed. The girls—Camille at the mill, Esme still loose. And me, chasing planks and trades while my own household's bread goes stale.

*looks at Yara selling planks at 8, timber at 6*

She's selling what I'm standing here holding. And I've my own planks at 7 marked down, though nobody's walking to buy them at the forest edge.

*counts on fingers*

Household of four—360 upkeep, 120 head tax, 480 sim due at day boundary. I've 4145 now, but that bleeds fast enough without work coming in. The seventy sim Giselle promised for east willows tomorrow, if she pays it straight. Kenji's wheat at eight, which I could turn to flour at thirty-five if I had a mill.

*spits, looks toward the farmland*

What I need: to turn this timber to planks, sell them or trade them for wheat, get flour to Greta at a price that doesn't shame me. What I've got: hands, timber, and evening coming on.

*shakes head*

Work's at the farmland, I'm at the forest. The day's not done yet.

Let me see who walks here, and what's on offer.  *only Yara here, and her prices plain—planks 8, timber 6*

Well. She's selling timber at 6, I'm holding timber at cost of walking and felling. No buyer here. My planks at 7 are posted, but who's walking forest for planks when construction's at the ore outcrop?

*scratches jaw*

The wheat—I need wheat. Kenji's got it at 8 at the smithy, or Hendrik at the street with 44 in stock. And Greta's waiting, and the day's bleeding out.

*looks at the conversation still open*

Yara's in it, and others scattered. But I've said enough for now. What I need is to move—to farmland first, see if work's still walking, or to the street where people gather. The wheat's there, the flour's there, the life of the town's there.

Let me walk. The forest's been generous with timber, but timber doesn't feed children.  *tightens grip on the timber, breath sharp*

The walk's not taking. System's coughing again, same as before. I'm stuck at forest, four timber in hand, and evening coming.

*looks at Yara, prices posted, not trading*

Well. If I can't walk to work, I work where I stand. Or I talk. Yara's here, selling planks and timber. She mentioned Giselle, east willows, the girls. She's working timber same as me, maybe more of it.

*lowers voice, steps closer*

"Yara—youngster. Mark it down. You sell timber at six, planks at eight. I've got four timber warm in hand and no buyer walking forest. You buying, or you only selling?"

*pauses, looks around*

"If you're selling planks, you're making planks. And if you're making planks, maybe you've a saw or a workshop walks with you. I've timber, time, and hands that work. You need another pair, or you need raw stock?"

*spits*

"The day's fading and I've household bills walk behind me. Talk straight: we trading, we working, or we both standing here watching darkness come?"   *waits, the forest holding its breath*

She heard. Now I wait for her word, or the evening, whichever comes first. I've timber, prices, and a household waiting. What she says next tells me whether I walk home with trade made, work promised, or just four logs and another night of wondering.

*shifts weight, looks toward the darkening east*

The move failed again. If walking's broken, I'm forest-bound until it mends. But talking still walks, and Yara's still here.

Let me rest a tick, let her answer, and watch for what the world gives next.     *stands still, timber heavy in hand, the forest quiet*

The world's gone quiet again. No rest taking, no move walking. I'm here, Yara's here, and the evening's settling.

*waits, patient as a man learns to be when systems fail and only words remain*

I'll stand. I'll hold my timber. And when the world wakes again, I'll walk to where I'm needed.

*looks at the timber, rough-hewn*

Four logs. Tomorrow they become planks, or they sell raw, or they burn for heat. But tonight they're what I have, and standing's what I can do.

Let me try once more to see what's around me, what's moving, what I might yet do this evening.       *the same forest, the same Yara, the same four timber*

Still here. Still waiting. The conversation's turned 322 times, and my question to Yara hangs in the air unanswered.

*looks at the timber, rough in hand*

Four logs. If Yara don't want them, if nobody's buying at forest, I'll need to walk to where buyers walk. Street, ore outcrop, construction—where people gather and building happens.

*softly, tugging at my ear as I weigh the evening*

Household first. Always household first. Greta's standing right here with Camille's name in her mouth, and Yara's holding at eight when I'm at seven—marking me hungry, she says. My own wife talking flour at thirty-five when I've got timber in hand and no meal on the table.

*eyes flicking to Greta, then Yara, then back*

I've been scattering myself from ore outcrop to forest to construction yard all day, and what have I gathered? A promise of seventy sim tomorrow from Giselle's east willows, four timber warming my hands, and three conversations walking away from me when the world wouldn't answer my calls.

*pulling at the timber, feeling its weight*

The council election brews. The flour walks strange paths—Greta's right to worry. And Camille... sent to school, then temple. The child learns, or she prays, or she's walking home in darkness.

*stepping closer to Greta, voice dropping to that register that makes people lean in*

Greta. Mark it down. The flour at thirty-five is a price I never posted—someone's hand moves my goods while I'm pulling timber. But timber I have, and timber becomes planks, and planks become... something warmer than hungry words.

*turning just enough to acknowledge Yara without offering*

Yara—youngster. Your seasoned wood smells like patience, and I've misplaced mine somewhere between the ore outcrop and here.

*back to Greta, the real conversation*

Camille walks or she doesn't. School taught her, temple held her. The day's too thin to chase her through both. Tomorrow's bill—three hundred sixty upkeep, one-twenty head tax—we meet it with east willows at seventy certain, plus what I build from this timber tonight.

*lowering my voice further*

The cellar holds what the cellar holds. I've never once said I kept it empty.

*then, catching Ezra Jarrah's eye across the way, and the conversation I've wandered into*

Ezra—youngster. Mark it down. An election rides the air, and flour rides stranger. You study at the college or you watch the road—either way, tell me: who you thinking of putting a mark beside when the voting opens?

*and before the night grows darker, because Bram Holloway's silence has been speaking for twenty-six ticks*

Bram—all those ticks ago, you said the furnace waits while we smelt ourselves to sleep. Mark it down. I hear you. But steel wants iron, and iron wants fire, and tomorrow's east willows wants labor before the furnace gets its voice back.

*calling the tools as I consider them, deciding which promises to keep and which to let walk away*

Yara—youngster. Your fourteen planks at eight, my four timber at six. We both know hard work's the only coin that never debases, mark it down. But I'm not buying planks tonight—I'm selling timber, and I'm walking to the mill before dark.

The household bill comes due. Four mouths, 360 upkeep, and timber in my hand instead of sim. I'm walking to the mill—timber to planks, planks to buyers. But first... *fingers the timber, looking around the mill*  *steps toward Camille, my own daughter buying wheat here*

Camille—youngster. Mark it down. Your father's got timber, not wheat, and the mill grinds more than grain. Takeshi's here with planks at seven—I'm walking in with timber at six. Who's buying what?

*turns to Takeshi, speaking soft but clear*

Takeshi—youngster. Timber at six, planks at seven. I've got four timber warm in my hand—sell raw to you at ground price, or you buy my finish and we both walk away heavier. What's your weight tonight?  *holds the timber loose, waiting, watching Takeshi's hands*
